stem: Which device is an example of an OSHA engineering control used to reduce occupational exposure to bloodborne pathogens?

options.A: A self-sheathing or retractable safety needle
options.B: A poster reminding staff not to recap needles
options.C: An annual lecture about sharps injuries without a device change
options.D: A staffing schedule that assigns injections to fewer nurses

rationale: OSHA defines engineering controls as controls that isolate or remove the bloodborne-pathogen hazard from the workplace and explicitly lists self-sheathing needles, sharps with engineered sharps injury protections, needleless systems, and sharps disposal containers as examples. Therefore A is correct. Posters, education, and staffing changes do not themselves constitute the device-based engineering control described here.
educational_objective: Identify safety-engineered sharps devices as engineering controls under OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard.
source_locator: §1910.1030(b) Definitions — Engineering Controls; Sharps with Engineered Sharps Injury Protections; §1910.1030(d)(2)(i) engineering and work-practice controls
source_claim_supported: Self-sheathing/retractable safety needles and other sharps with engineered injury protections are examples of OSHA engineering controls that isolate or remove bloodborne-pathogen hazards.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)

correction_summary: Simplified the item to the exact OSHA definition and removed wording that could imply a particular safety device is mandatory for every procedure regardless of feasibility and appropriateness.
audit_findings: A is an explicit OSHA example. B and C are education/work-practice approaches rather than an engineering device; D is administrative staffing. No second-answer ambiguity, cueing or unsupported universal requirement remains.
